stem:
Esha writes the up-and-down sum $1+2+3+4+5+6+5+4+3+2+1$ with consecutive counting numbers that climb from $1$ to $6$ and then fall back to $1$. The figure shows those counts filling a $6$-by-$6$ square of unit tiles. She is checking why this sum equals $6^{2}$, not a triangular or hexagonal number sum.

Why does that sum equal $6^{2}$?

options.text: The consecutive climb and fall from $1$ to $6$ fill the $6$-by-$6$ square of unit tiles, so the sum is $36$.
Any climb-and-fall list of numbers fills a $6$-by-$6$ square, even when the numbers are not consecutive counting numbers from $1$.
Filling the $6$-by-$6$ square of unit tiles is what produces the consecutive counting numbers from $1$ to $6$.
The same filling also makes a triangular or hexagonal number sum equal $36$.

teacher.key_rationale: The up-and-down consecutive counts from 1 to 6 pair into a 6-by-6 square, so the sum is 36. Dropping the consecutive-from-1 condition, reversing square-from-counts, or extending the rule to triangular/hexagonal sums are wrong about that fill.
teacher.figure_note: Rewrote source kite-on-grid as a 6-by-6 unit-tile square for the up-and-down sum.
